design_detail: Critical narrative review of sex differences (biological) and gender differences (socially determined roles), using the NIH Office of Research on Women's Health definitions, across substance use disorders: biology (metabolism, subjective effects, ovarian hormones, neuroimaging), US epidemiology (mainly 2015 National Survey on Drug Use and Health figures), course of illness including telescoping, consequences and co-occurring disorders, treatment seeking, treatment outcome, gender-specific treatment, and pregnancy. Search terms were adapted from the authors' group's 2007 review (greenfield_2007), whose methods are not repeated; treatment papers were limited to 2007 to April 2017, and government survey reports and earlier 'seminal' papers were added; 517 papers were reviewed for relevance. No inclusion criteria, appraisal tool, flow diagram or pooling. Focus on human studies; preclinical work referred elsewhere.
can_establish: What the authors' group, updating its 2007 review, judged the main human findings on sex and gender differences in substance use disorders to be as of April 2017, with US prevalence figures from national surveys and pointers to the primary studies on telescoping, treatment entry, treatment outcome and gender-specific treatment.
cannot_establish: The size or certainty of any sex or gender difference (no systematic selection, no appraisal of the cited studies, no pooling); whether differences are caused by sex, by gender or by who reaches treatment (the cited designs rarely separate them); or whether the selection of studies is complete.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Literature found with search terms adapted from Greenfield, Brooks et al. (2007), plus US government survey publications for prevalence and earlier papers chosen as seminal for biology, aetiology and pregnancy (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond date limits: treatment papers published 2007 to April 2017; papers before 2007 allowed for aetiology and pregnancy. The databases are not named in this paper (the reader is referred to the 2007 review). The text nonetheless cites some treatment studies from before 2007 (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own, from 517 papers reviewed for relevance by unstated criteria. Many findings on women's greater impairment, comorbidity and faster progression come from treatment samples, which the review itself warns may over-represent women with more severe disorders (Course of Illness, 1st paragraph). Several treatment studies discussed are the authors' own.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. For sex and gender comparisons the review does not say, study by study, whether samples were treatment or general-population samples (except for telescoping, where it contrasts the two), how the timing of first use, problems and treatment was measured (recalled or recorded as it happened), or what was adjusted for.
exposure.polysubstance: Named as an understudied area in women (Discussion, 6th paragraph); not otherwise addressed.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women, and women with women by subgroup (pregnant, postpartum, with co-occurring disorders), as in the cited studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The review notes that prospective studies measuring differences before drug exposure are needed to tell sex differences in biology from consequences of use (Biological Sex Differences, 8th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies; not described in the review.
outcomes.operationalization: Sex as biological difference and gender as socially determined roles that vary across cultures and over time (NIH Office of Research on Women's Health); telescoping as faster progression from initiation to problems and from problems to treatment seeking.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited; none pooled. US 2015 (NSDUH, ages 12 and older), women vs men: past-month alcohol use 47.4% vs 56.2%; binge drinking 20.5% vs 29.6%; heavy drinking 4.2% vs 8.9%; alcohol use disorder 4.1% vs 7.8%; past-month illicit drug use 7.9% vs 12.5%; illicit drug use disorder 2% vs 3.8%; adults' prescription drug misuse 2.2% vs 2.7%. Ages 12–17: alcohol 9.9% of girls vs 9.6% of boys, binge drinking 5.8% in both, illicit drugs 8.8% in both. Treatment received among people needing it (2015): 10.4% of women vs 11.1% of men. Trials: COMBINE (N=1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (N=653, 40% women) found no gender differences in outcome; smoking cessation meta-analysis of 32 trials (N=14,389, 51% women). Mortality in clinical-trial participants with substance use disorders relative to the general population: about 5-fold in women and 3-fold in men, difference not significant.
analysis.selective_reporting: Gender-specific treatment is presented as supported, but the evidence summarized for women-only against mixed-gender programmes in general is mostly observational (programme comparisons), randomized support is cited only for programmes designed for particular groups of women, and the authors' own larger randomized trial found the women-focused group as effective as mixed-gender counselling, not better; null findings (Bride, 2001) are explained by programme features. Biological findings are described as consistent where they rest on few studies.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level; the review notes that many neuroimaging studies did not test sex differences or were underpowered, and that trials stratify by gender but rarely analyse it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A broad summary in which: women in the US use alcohol and illicit drugs less than men but the gap is closing or absent in adolescents; women start using later on average; faster progression in women (telescoping) has been reported mainly in treatment samples and was not found in a general-population analysis (keyes_2010); women in treatment report more functional impairment and more anxiety, depression and trauma; women are less often treated for alcohol use disorder but treatment entry for drug use disorders is more equal; most large trials show no gender difference in outcome or retention, smoking cessation being the exception, and most of the medicine-specific differences listed go against women; women-only programmes are associated with better outcomes in observational comparisons, while the authors' own larger trial found equivalence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that adverse medical, psychiatric and functional consequences are often more severe in women and that men and women do not substantively differ in treatment outcomes; the Discussion infers that much of the historical gender gap in prevalence may have been social and cultural rather than biological. Gaps: (1) the 'more severe consequences' statement rests largely on treatment samples, to which the review's own caution about telescoping (women in treatment may have more severe disorders) applies equally but is not applied; (2) the abstract's statement that gender contributes to initiation and course is causal in form, while the support is associations, including an ecological association between gender-role traditionality and the size of the gender gap across countries; (3) the statement that men and women do not differ in likelihood of use once access is controlled is generalized from three cited studies; (4) the telescoping paragraph lists replications but cites, for marijuana, a paper whose reference-list title concerns alcohol dependence (see reporting issues). The wording is otherwise hedged ('may', 'suggest'), and the Discussion is explicit about gaps and under-representation of women in trials.

timeline.event: Project MATCH telescoping study, cited by McHugh et al. as a replication of telescoping in alcohol.
The authors' group's earlier review of treatment entry, retention and outcome in women, whose search terms this review reuses.
General-population analysis of two US surveys, cited as failing to replicate telescoping.
NESARC transition analysis, cited for greater nicotine and lower cannabis dependence liability in women.
Becker, McClellan and Reed (2017) review, cited for the explanation that telescoping appears in treatment samples but not in population surveys.
Marks and Clark critique the telescoping concept as rooted in gender bias.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely used overview that updates greenfield_2007; for each question its claims need the primary studies. On telescoping it gives both sides and the treatment-versus-population explanation; on treatment outcome its conclusion of no substantive difference (apart from smoking cessation) matches the 2007 review.

funding.funder: Role of Funding Sources: NIDA grants UG1 DA015831 (Greenfield and McHugh) and K23 DA035297 (McHugh); NIDA had no further role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Under Author Disclosures, the Conflict of Interest statement says that all other authors declare no conflicts of interest; no declaration for any particular author precedes it in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Division of Alcohol and Drug Abuse, McLean Hospital, and Department of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School. The authors (notably Greenfield and McHugh) wrote several of the treatment studies discussed, including the COMBINE gender analysis, a prescription-opioid trial analysis and the Women's Recovery Group trials of their own women-focused group therapy; recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: For telescoping and consequences, prospective general-population cohorts of women and men that record use, problems and treatment as they happen and measure sex (including hormonal status) and gender (roles, access, stigma) separately; for treatment, trials powered in advance for sex-by-treatment interactions; and systematic reviews with explicit criteria and appraisal for each question.

domains.note: Search terms and date limits are given and 517 papers were reviewed, but the databases are not named here, no inclusion criteria or flow are reported, prevalence sources and 'seminal' older papers were chosen by the authors, and pre-2007 treatment studies appear despite the stated limit.

No formal appraisal; some limits are named (cross-sectional imaging cannot show causality; underpowered imaging; women under-represented in disulfiram trials; survey items missing childcare barriers), but most findings are given without design or sample.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The treatment sections lean on the group's own work (the 2007 review, COMBINE and prescription-opioid analyses, the Women's Recovery Group trials).
Mostly hedged, but some statements are made as settled on few studies (greater intoxication in women from gastric enzyme and body water; no sex difference in use once access is controlled).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against sex and gender differences
domains.note: Telescoping is presented with both sides; for gender-specific treatment, the equivalence result of the authors' own larger trial and null programme comparisons are under-weighted relative to observational benefits.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high, set by the unsystematic selection. The review is useful as a map: it may be cited for the US prevalence figures it reports from named national surveys (better cited to the surveys themselves), for the statement that telescoping has been found mainly in treatment samples and not in a population-based analysis, and as pointers to primary studies. It should not be the sole support for any claim about the size or cause of a sex or gender difference; claims should rest on the primary studies or on systematic reviews.

key_findings.finding: Methods: a critical review using search terms adapted from the authors' 2007 review (methods not repeated here), with treatment papers limited to 2007 through April 2017, added US government survey reports and earlier seminal papers for aetiology and pregnancy; 517 papers were reviewed for relevance. Sex is defined as biological difference and gender as socially determined roles.

Alcohol: women have lower gastric alcohol dehydrogenase activity and lower total body water than men, giving higher blood alcohol concentrations and greater intoxication after the same amount (as cited: Baraona et al., 2001; Chrostek et al., 2003). Sex differences in the metabolism of other drugs have not been consistently shown; some evidence suggests faster nicotine metabolism and higher peak plasma cocaine in women.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Stated as settled on two citations; the project's reading list flags that the gastric-enzyme explanation was contested (Ammon et al., 1996), which this review does not mention.

key_findings.finding: Subjective drug effects show no consistent sex difference: some laboratory studies found none, others greater effects in men or in women. In two laboratory studies (as cited), women gave higher abuse-liability ratings at the lowest doses tested of THC (5 mg; no route given) and d-amphetamine (8–10 mg), and men at the higher doses tested (15 mg THC; 16–20 mg d-amphetamine); one study found greater THC effects in men than women only among people who did not use cannabis often.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Doses are the laboratory study conditions as cited, not guidance of any kind.

key_findings.finding: Menstrual-cycle findings are inconsistent (greater liking in the follicular than luteal phase in some studies, none in others); given progesterone has more consistent effects, reducing cue-induced cocaine craving and nicotine craving, and was associated with less cocaine relapse in postpartum women (one trial) and less nicotine relapse in a small pilot.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Neuroimaging: many studies did not detect, did not test, or were underpowered to test sex differences; cross-sectional volume differences cannot show causality; single studies report higher striatal dopamine release in men than women after stimulants, alcohol and nicotine. The authors add that these differences may reflect gender as well as sex, and that prospective studies are needed to tell pre-existing differences from effects of use.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 5th–8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: US prevalence, 2015 NSDUH (ages 12 and older), women vs men: past-month alcohol 47.4% vs 56.2%; binge drinking (4+ drinks for women, 5+ for men) 20.5% vs 29.6%; heavy drinking 4.2% vs 8.9%; alcohol use disorder 4.1% vs 7.8%; past-month illicit drug use 7.9% vs 12.5%; illicit drug use disorder 2% vs 3.8%. Ages 12–17: alcohol 9.9% of girls vs 9.6% of boys, binge drinking 5.8% in both, illicit drugs 8.8% in both, prescription drug misuse 2.3% vs 1.7%. Adults' prescription drug misuse 2.2% vs 2.7%.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Prevalence and Incidence, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Trends: the gender gap in substance use disorders is narrowing; binge drinking among US women over 60 rose 3.7% a year (1997–2014) with no change in men; heroin use rose 100% in women vs 50% in men (2002–2013); past-year cannabis use rose more in men (+4.4% vs +2.7%; 16.9% vs 10.1% in 2014). Across countries (WHO World Mental Health Surveys), less traditional gender roles go with a smaller gap; men have more access to drugs, and in three cited studies the chance of use did not differ by sex once access (opportunity) was controlled.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Prevalence and Incidence, 1st, 2nd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Telescoping: women on average start using later (Greenfield et al., 2010; keyes_2010); faster progression in women has been reported for alcohol (Diehl et al., 2007; Randall et al., 1999), marijuana, cocaine (Haas and Peters, 2000, in drug-involved offenders) and prescription opioids, but not for heroin (Lewis et al., 2014; Stoltman et al., 2015), and a large population-based analysis of alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010) did not find it. Citing a 2017 review, the authors explain the discrepancy by sample: telescoping has been found mainly in women already in treatment, who likely have more severe disorders, and not in population surveys; a subset of women may progress rapidly.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The review does not say how timing was measured or what was adjusted for in the studies it lists.

key_findings.finding: Dependence liability varies modestly by gender: greater for nicotine and lower for cannabis in women than men (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011; Wagner and Anthony, 2007); heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine use follow a chronic course of persistent regular use in both sexes (one cited cohort), and treatment, especially early and sustained, is associated with a better course in both.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No definition of chronic course or remission and no description of the cited cohorts are given.

key_findings.finding: Consequences: women in treatment report more severe impairment in employment, family and social, medical and psychiatric functioning and poorer quality of life; men report more legal problems (mixed). Mortality among women with alcohol use disorders was four times the general population in one 1983 follow-up; prescription-opioid overdose deaths rose 400% in women vs 265% in men since 1999; among people in substance use disorder treatment (the cited source is, by its title, a pooled analysis of 22 Clinical Trials Network trials), mortality was about 5-fold the general population in women and 3-fold in men, a difference that was not significant.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Adverse Consequences and Co-occurring Psychiatric Disorders, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Co-occurring disorders: anxiety and depressive disorders are more common in women with substance use disorders, conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder in men; women more often report trauma and PTSD beginning before the substance use disorder and more often use substances to relieve negative feelings.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Adverse Consequences and Co-occurring Psychiatric Disorders, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Treatment seeking: some studies find women reach treatment sooner after first use and after onset; in 2015, 10.4% of an estimated 7.9 million US women who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it, against 11.1% of men; under-use is most marked among women with alcohol use disorder; men more often receive specialized addiction treatment and women more often mental-health care. Gender was not associated with past-year treatment use for illicit drug use disorders (Compton et al., 2007, a NESARC analysis by its reference title), and women were 46.8% of 2014 admissions for primary prescription-opioid use disorder.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Treatment outcome: most large randomized trials found no gender difference in outcome, for example COMBINE for alcohol dependence (N=1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (N=653, 40% women). The exception is smoking cessation, with worse outcomes in women; in a meta-analysis of 32 trials (N=14,389, 51% women) varenicline worked as well in both sexes against placebo, with women benefiting more relative to nicotine replacement and bupropion. Behavioural treatments and mutual-help groups worked similarly in women and men; the efficacy of disulfiram for alcohol use disorder in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 2nd–5th paragraphs; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Retention: an aggregation of 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (N>11,000) found no difference in retention by gender, and an analysis of over 1.7 million US treatment episodes found no difference in completion except that women less often completed detoxification.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Gender-specific treatment: across 43 programmes, women in women-only programmes had better drug-use outcomes than women in mixed-gender programmes despite greater severity; other comparisons found modest benefits; a programme that switched to single-gender groups without other changes found none. The authors' own Women's Recovery Group gave greater reductions at 6 months in a small closed-group trial, and in a larger rolling-group trial was as effective as mixed-gender counselling. Women-only treatment is also associated with less criminal activity and incarceration after treatment (two cited studies, designs not described), and several randomized trials are cited as supporting gender-specific treatment for particular groups of women: women with children, women with co-occurring psychiatric disorders and women in the criminal justice system.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy: from NSDUH (CBHSQ, 2016), past-month illicit drug use 4.7%, tobacco 13.9%, alcohol 9.3% and any substance 21.7% of pregnant women; about 3.6% of pregnant women meet criteria for alcohol use disorder and 1.6% for a drug use disorder (cited to Vesga-Lopez et al., 2008, not to NSDUH); only 8.7% of pregnant women with substance use disorders receive specialized treatment (Terplan et al., 2012); 6.8% of treatment facilities offer childcare (SAMHSA, 2017).
key_findings.locator: Substance Use in Pregnancy, 1st paragraph; Treatments for Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the narrowing gender gap over three decades suggests much of the historical difference may have been social and cultural rather than biological; sex differences robust in animal models are much less so in humans; most large trials stratify by gender but do not analyse it; in a review of structural neuroimaging studies, almost three-quarters did not evaluate sex differences.

Gender differences in response to particular medicines (as cited): nicotine replacement worked better in men in a large randomized study (Perkins and Scott, 2008); varenicline worked better in women in one meta-analysis (McKee et al., 2016) and, in another, as well in both sexes against placebo but with more benefit for women relative to nicotine patch and bupropion; with naltrexone for smoking, men cut down more and women gained less weight; women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence (DeVito et al., 2014); naltrexone findings for alcohol dependence were mixed (men responded better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE); no gender difference with buprenorphine or methadone; women did worse than men with buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine dependence, although buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Most of the differences listed go against women (nicotine replacement, smoking reduction with naltrexone, disulfiram for cocaine, buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine); varenicline and smaller weight gain with naltrexone are in women's favour. The abstract's and Discussion's summary of no substantive difference apart from smoking cessation leaves them out.

reporting_issues.issue: Telescoping in marijuana is cited to 'Khan, Okuda, et al., 2013', whose reference-list entry is a NESARC paper on gender differences in lifetime alcohol dependence; the cannabis paper is Khan, Secades-Villa et al. (2013), cited correctly elsewhere in the review.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: The marijuana telescoping evidence should be traced to the cannabis paper; whether the alcohol paper, a general-population analysis, reports telescoping is not stated and would bear on the treatment-versus-population explanation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conflict of Interest statement says that 'all other authors' declare no conflicts, but no declaration by any author precedes it in the author manuscript (the Author Disclosures heading is followed only by Contributors).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Author Disclosures › Conflict of Interest
reporting_issues.consequence: Declared interests cannot be fully recorded from this version; the published version should be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Treatment papers are said to be limited to 2007–April 2017, but the treatment sections cite earlier studies (Linehan et al., 1999; Najavits et al., 1998; Orwin et al., 2001; Bride, 2001).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Introduction (untitled), 2nd paragraph; Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated selection rule was not followed, which confirms that selection was by judgment.

reporting_issues.issue: Blanco et al. (2013) is cited both for women reaching treatment sooner after onset and for no gender difference in treatment entry for prescription-opioid use disorder; the review does not say whether these refer to speed and to probability respectively.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about women's speed of entry into treatment need the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Keyes et al. (2010) is cited for 'other studies' not finding telescoping across cohorts, right after being cited as the population-based analysis; the reference list also gives Seedat et al. (2009) twice as 2009a and 2009b with identical details; small editing slips ('malesmen', 'sex gender differences').
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph; Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 2nd and 7th paragraphs; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the general-population evidence against telescoping cited here is one analysis, not several.

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol use in pregnancy is given as 9.3% 'including 4.6% and 0.8% with heavy use', without saying what the two figures measure.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Substance Use in Pregnancy, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The two sub-figures cannot be cited without the NSDUH source.
